title: Agent Communication Protocols
summary: When multiple agents work together, they don't share a brain — they exchange messages. A communication protocol defines the shape of those messages (sender, recipient, role, content), who speaks when (turn-taking), and how information is preserved instead of degrading like a game of telephone. Get the protocol right and a crew coordinates; get it wrong and agents talk past each other or amplify each other's mistakes.

subtopics.title: Messages are structured, not raw text
subtopics.explanation: In a single agent, the model just reads a chat history; in a multi-agent system, every exchange is a typed message with a sender, a recipient, a role, and a content payload so the routing layer knows who said what to whom. Freeform strings passed between agents lose provenance — you can't tell later whether 'the answer' came from the researcher or the critic. A structured message envelope is the foundation every other protocol decision is built on.
subtopics.example:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Message:
    sender: str          # "researcher"
    recipient: str       # "writer" or "all"
    role: str            # "proposal" | "critique" | "result"
    content: str

# an explicit envelope keeps provenance intact
msg = Message(
    sender="researcher",
    recipient="writer",
    role="result",
    content="Found 3 sources on quarterly churn.",
)
# the router can now decide who gets this and why

subtopics.title: Roles and addressing decide who receives what
subtopics.explanation: Each agent has a role (planner, worker, critic) and messages are addressed either to one recipient or broadcast to all. Addressing controls information flow: a critique aimed only at the writer keeps the planner's context clean, while a broadcast result lets everyone update. Deciding what each agent needs to see — and hiding what it doesn't — is how you stop context windows from bloating and agents from drowning in irrelevant chatter.
subtopics.example:
def route(msg, agents):
    # direct address -> one recipient; "all" -> broadcast
    if msg.recipient == "all":
        return [a for a in agents if a.name != msg.sender]
    return [a for a in agents if a.name == msg.recipient]

agents = [planner, writer, critic]
critique = Message("critic", "writer", "critique", "Intro is too long.")
recipients = route(critique, agents)
# only the writer sees the critique; planner's context stays lean

subtopics.title: Turn-taking prevents chaos
subtopics.explanation: Without a rule for who speaks next, agents either all respond at once (wasting tokens on duplicated work) or wait on each other forever. Turn-taking policies — round-robin, a manager that nominates the next speaker, or reply-to-sender — impose order on the conversation. A clear speaker-selection policy is what turns a pile of agents into a coordinated conversation rather than a shouting match.

subtopics.title: Standard protocols give a shared contract
subtopics.explanation: Rather than inventing an envelope per project, teams adopt shared conventions — an OpenAI-style role/content message list, or emerging cross-vendor specs like MCP for tool/context exchange and agent-to-agent messaging standards — so heterogeneous agents can interoperate. A standard is just an agreed schema plus semantics for the fields. Speaking a common protocol is what lets agents built by different teams (or vendors) plug into the same conversation without custom glue.
subtopics.example:
# a portable, provider-agnostic message list
conversation = [
    {"role": "system", "name": "manager", "content": "Coordinate the crew."},
    {"role": "assistant", "name": "researcher", "content": "Sources gathered."},
    {"role": "assistant", "name": "writer", "content": "Draft ready for review."},
]
# 'name' distinguishes agents while 'role' stays protocol-standard
for m in conversation:
    print(f"{m.get('name', m['role'])}: {m['content']}")

subtopics.title: Avoiding telephone-game degradation
subtopics.explanation: When agent B summarizes agent A, and C summarizes B, each hop lossily rephrases the original and small errors compound into confident nonsense — the classic telephone game. Defenses include passing the original artifact (not a summary of a summary), pinning source-of-truth facts, and having a verifier compare a downstream claim against the original. Preserving the ground truth across hops is the difference between a crew that refines an answer and one that hallucinates its way off a cliff.

foundations.overview: A multi-agent system is a set of LLM-driven agents that cooperate by exchanging messages, because no agent can see inside another's reasoning. A communication protocol is the contract governing those exchanges: the structured message envelope (who sent it, who should receive it, what kind of message it is, and its content), the addressing and role scheme that controls information flow, the turn-taking policy that decides who speaks next, and the discipline that keeps information from degrading as it hops between agents. Adopting a shared/standard protocol lets agents from different teams or vendors interoperate. The through-line is that coordination quality is bounded by communication quality — a crew is only as good as the messages it passes.
foundations.formalDefinition: An agent communication protocol is a specification of (1) a message schema — the fields every inter-agent message carries (sender, recipient, role/type, content), (2) an addressing and routing scheme (direct vs broadcast), (3) a turn-taking / speaker-selection policy, and (4) semantics for interpreting each field — such that independent agents can exchange information deterministically and preserve provenance across the conversation.
foundations.whyItMatters: In single-agent systems the 'conversation' is just the model's own history; in multi-agent systems the conversation IS the system, so its structure determines whether agents coordinate or collide. Poorly defined messaging produces telephone-game errors, duplicated work, runaway token cost, and deadlocks — the failure modes that make naive multi-agent demos worse than a single agent.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a project team using a shared ticketing system instead of shouting across the room. Every ticket has an author, an assignee, a type, and a description (the message schema); tickets are assigned to one person or the whole team (addressing); there's a rule for who picks up the next ticket (turn-taking); and everyone links back to the original spec rather than to a coworker's paraphrase (avoiding telephone-game drift).
foundations.realWorldUsage: Research crews where a planner delegates to searchers and a writer synthesizes, code-review setups where a coder and a critic exchange proposals and critiques, customer-support routing where a triage agent hands structured tickets to specialists, and cross-vendor agent ecosystems that exchange tool/context messages over shared protocols like MCP.
commonUseCases: Coder + critic exchanging proposals and critiques
Broadcast results updating a whole crew at once
Cross-vendor agents interoperating over a shared protocol

commonMisconceptions.myth: Agents can just pass plain text to each other like a chat.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Plain text loses provenance and routing information. A structured envelope (sender, recipient, role, content) is what lets the system know who said what and who should receive it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More agents talking always produces a better answer.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Without turn-taking and drift control, extra hops mostly add cost and compound errors (the telephone game). Coordination quality is bounded by communication quality, not agent count.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every agent should see every message.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Broadcasting everything bloats context windows and buries relevant signals in noise. Good protocols address messages deliberately and hide what an agent doesn't need.

interactiveWidget.title: The telephone game, in agents
interactiveWidget.caption: A note on why message structure and drift control matter more than the number of agents you add.

config.note: Picture three agents in a line. The researcher finds a fact: 'Q3 churn was 4.2%, driven mainly by the SMB segment.' The analyst, told only to 'summarize', writes 'churn rose, mostly small customers.' The writer, summarizing that, produces 'churn is climbing among small businesses' — the specific 4.2% and the word 'Q3' are gone, and 'was' has quietly become 'is climbing.' No agent lied; each just lossily rephrased the last hop. That is telephone-game degradation, and it is the default behavior of a naive multi-agent chain. Two protocol choices prevent it. First, structure every message so provenance survives: instead of a bare string, each hop carries {sender, recipient, role, content} and, critically, a pinned source_of_truth. Second, make downstream agents summarize the ORIGINAL artifact, not the previous agent's summary — or add a verifier whose only job is to check a final claim against the source. The lesson that surprises people: adding agents does not add intelligence, it adds hops, and every hop is a chance to lose or distort information. A single agent with the full context often beats a chain of agents each holding a blurry photocopy. Reach for multiple agents when the work genuinely parallelizes or needs distinct roles (a critic really does catch things a writer misses) — and when you do, invest in the message schema and drift control first, because coordination quality is capped by communication quality.

checkpoints.prompt: Why do inter-agent messages use a structured envelope (sender, recipient, role, content) instead of plain text?
options: Plain text is slower to transmit
To preserve provenance and let the router decide who receives what
Because LLMs can't read plain strings
It's required by the OpenAI API
checkpoints.explanation: A structured envelope keeps track of who said what to whom (provenance) and gives the routing layer the fields it needs to address messages. Plain text loses that information the moment it's passed on.

checkpoints.prompt: With round-robin turn-taking over [planner, writer, critic], if the last speaker was 'writer', who speaks next?
checkpoints.explanation: index('writer') is 1, (1 + 1) % 3 = 2, and names[2] is 'critic'. Round-robin simply advances to the next agent in the list, wrapping around at the end.

checkpoints.prompt: A chain of agents each summarizing the previous agent's summary produces confidently wrong output. What's the best fix?
options: Add more summarizing agents to average out errors
Raise the temperature so agents are more creative
Have each agent summarize the pinned original artifact, or add a verifier against the source
checkpoints.explanation: That's telephone-game degradation: each hop lossily rephrases the last. Carrying a pinned source-of-truth and summarizing the original (or verifying downstream claims against it) preserves ground truth across hops.

keyTakeaways: In multi-agent systems the conversation IS the system — coordination quality is bounded by communication quality.
Use a structured message envelope (sender, recipient, role, content) so provenance and routing survive every hop.
Addressing and roles control information flow: direct-address to keep context lean, broadcast to update everyone.
A turn-taking policy (round-robin, manager-nominated, reply-to) turns a pile of agents into an ordered conversation.
Prevent telephone-game drift by pinning a source-of-truth and summarizing the original — not the previous hop's guess.
